newsitem.title: USA: Stocks hit 10th 1997 record, bonds firm.
newsitem.headline: Stocks hit 10th 1997 record, bonds firm.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's upbeat remarks on the economy Tuesday propelled blue-chip stocks to their 10th record close this year and sparked a rally in the bond market.
The dollar rose against the German mark on positive remarks by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, but edged lower vs. the Japanaese yen.
Crude and heating oil prices fell as milder weather spread across the northern states.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 40.03 points at 6,883.90, beating Monday's high of 6,843.87. The technology-laced Nasdaq Composite index, the Standard & Poor's composite and the NYSE Composite all set new highs.

The markets focused on Greenspan's scheduled appearance Tuesday morning before the Senate to testify on the state of the economy. Although he warned about the risks of wage-driven inflation, Greenspan said the economy showed vigour and little sign of inflationary tensions.

"Greenspan's speech was much more market-friendly than the comments he's previously made and the comments made recently by some other Fed officials," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
Last year, Greenspan's warning of "irrational exuberance" triggered a plunge in financial markets worldwide.
Soon after Greenspan's testimony, bonds rallied, giving stocks the green light to resume their torrid climb.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose more than half a point, or $5.31 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.79 percent from Friday's close of 6.83 percent. The yield and the price move in opposite directions.
The bond market was closed Monday for the Martin Luther King Jr. holiday.
In currency markets, the dollar rose against the mark after Treasury Secretary Rubin told reporters in Washington he was not concerned a strong dollar would hurt U.S. exporters.
But the dollar slipped against the yen early in the session after comments from Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who called the yen's recent slide "excessive" and "undesirable."
The dollar ended higher at 1.6296 marks vs. 1.6252 at Monday's close, but edged lower to 117.91 Japanese yen from 118.05.

Crude and heating oil prices fell as higher temperatures warmed the northern United States. At the New York Mercantile Exchange, February heating oil closed 0.91 cent a gallon lower at 66.03 cents. February crude oil ended 43 cents a barrel lower at $24.80.
Gasoline bucked the lower trend, with February unleaded gasoline rising 0.21 cent a gallon to 67.44 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index recovered from a near 30-point decline to finish the day 1.5 points higher at 4,195.5. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 finished down 122.18 points at 17,358.16.
